title: Abu Talib's shield
hookLine: his uncle never accepts Islam, yet protects him to the end

lines: I WILL NEVER HAND YOU OVER.
cards: We left a nephew in tears, getting up to leave his uncle's house. He has just refused the sun and the moon. His uncle has just asked him to spare them both.
Now Abu Talib calls him back. He has every reason to step aside: the leaders of his own tribe are angry with him.
Ibn Ishaq gives his words: go, son of my brother, and say what you like; by Allah, I will never hand you over. Today: Banu Hashim.

teach.b: Abu Talib had taken the boy in after his grandfather died, and raised him with his own children, Ali among them.
As the sirah tells it, Abu Talib stood at the head of the Banu Hashim, and while he stood behind his nephew, Quraysh could not simply take him. Quraysh tried to get around it.
The sirah tells of a strange offer: they brought him a handsome young man of their own, Umarah ibn al-Walid, and said, take him as your son, and hand us your nephew.

teach.h: YOUR SON TO FEED, MINE TO KILL?
teach.b: Abu Talib's answer, in Ibn Ishaq: you give me your son to feed, and I give you mine to kill? He refused. Then comes the question of his own faith.
In Sunni sources, including al-Bukhari, Abu Talib is reported to have died without accepting Islam. Shia tradition holds that he was a believer who kept it hidden to protect his nephew.
The two readings differ, and both remember him with honor for what he did.
Either way, the outward story is the same: a man who did not publicly follow the message stood between it and harm, at a cost to his standing among his own people.
This week has been about people around the Prophet: Abu Bakr believing at once, al-Arqam opening his house, the quiet season, Safa, the uncle who cursed. Two uncles, two sons of Abd al-Muttalib.
One cursed him in front of the clans.

teach.h: I WILL NEVER HAND YOU OVER.
teach.b: The other said: I will never hand you over.

how: Muslims remember Abu Talib's protection of the Prophet in sirah study; Sunni and Shia Muslims differ on his faith, and both speak of his loyalty with honor.

practice: Think of someone who stood up for you, or made room for you, though they didn't share your choices: a parent of a different faith, a boss who disagreed but backed you, a friend who said, I don't get it, but I'm with you.
Name quietly what it cost them, an argument, some standing, a worry kept to themselves. If you pray, ask good for them.

wordCard.voice: Banu Hashim. The clan Abu Talib led, which meant Quraysh could not simply take his nephew while he stood behind him. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: protected by love. A week of people around him, ending with an uncle's wall. That's day seven hundred thirty-five.
